claims.label: Unity of type is explained by unity of descent
claims.statement: The fundamental agreement in structure among organisms of the same class, independent of their habits of life, is explained by their common descent.

operationalizations.text: Test for hierarchical congruence (tree-to-tree similarity and shared monophyly) between phylogenies inferred from homologous anatomical 'unity of type' characters and independent phylogenies inferred from neutral genomic sequences across organisms within major classes, regardless of ecological guild.

Test whether shared structural plans covary with independently inferred common ancestry more strongly than with present ecology, using morphological and molecular phylogenies. Nested homology matching ancestry supports the claim; repeated ecology-based grouping independent of ancestry opposes it.

Within a class, compare a morphological distance matrix of fundamental structure with a molecular tree and with ecological similarity. Agreement with the molecular tree, and not with habits of life, supports unity of descent; grouping by habit rather than by independent genealogy would refute that explanation.

obstacles: Evaluating 'unity of type is explained by unity of descent' requires avoiding circularity by comparing morphological homology trees against independent molecular sequence trees and testing against non-genealogical null models (e.g., purely functional/ecological clustering).
Some morphological characters also inform classifications and can create circularity.
Some classes still have sparse morphological matrices or molecule-poor regions of the tree.
Particular characters can be conserved by constraint even when the nested body plan fits descent.

claims.label: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species
claims.statement: Species are not independently created and immutable; species of the same genus are lineal descendants of some other, generally extinct, species, just as varieties of one species descend from that species.

operationalizations.text: Test for statistically significant hierarchical tree structure (phylogenetic signal, shared derived endogenous retroviruses/pseudogenes, and congruence between independent genomic loci and stratigraphic order) among congeneric species versus a null model of independent origin.

Compare independent molecular characters, shared derived genomic changes and fossil succession against separate-creation and common-descent models. Nested congruent ancestry across congeneric species supports descent; independent origins without shared history would refute it.

Test whether species placed in the same genus form clades on sequence data, using concordance across independent loci rather than a single assumed tree, and whether the inferred ancestral node is older than the living members and matched by extinct fossil relatives. Independent creation or immutability would be favoured if genetic similarity were not hierarchically nested or if living species were routinely ancestral to their congeners; shared ancestry from earlier, now extinct lineages would favour the historical claim.

obstacles: Incomplete lineage sorting and introgression create local gene-tree discordance within rapidly radiating genera.
Fossil ancestors are rarely identifiable with certainty.
Not every described species has genomic data.
Genus limits are themselves revised using phylogenies, so a test must freeze a pre-molecular classification or use rank-free clades.
Many named genera still lack sequence data, and the fossil record is sparse for soft-bodied groups and plants.
Hybrid speciation and incomplete lineage sorting produce local non-monophyly without restoring independent creation.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.label: Long ages of abundant life preceded the lowest Silurian strata
claims.statement: If descent with modification is true, periods at least as long as the whole time from the Silurian to the present must have passed before the lowest Silurian strata were laid down, and during them the world swarmed with living creatures.

operationalizations.text: Compare the radiometric duration of the fossiliferous Precambrian (Archean and Proterozoic eons) with the Phanerozoic (Cambrian/Silurian to present), and evaluate the global stratigraphic and geochemical record of Precambrian life.

Estimate the age and diversity of pre-Silurian life from radiometrically dated fossils, biomarkers, and molecular-clock analyses. Compare the duration before the Silurian and evidence of abundance with the Silurian-to-present interval and a minimal-life alternative.

Compare the radiometric duration before Darwin's lowest fossiliferous strata, mapped to the base of the Cambrian, with the duration from that horizon to the present, and score whether fossils or biomarkers show widespread life through the earlier interval. A shorter pre-Cambrian span, or a span lacking evidence of life, would refute the claim.

obstacles: Interpreting whether predominantly microbial and Ediacaran ecosystems satisfy Darwin's phrase 'swarmed with living creatures' involves minor semantic latitude.
Early molecular clocks have broad calibration uncertainty.
Soft-bodied Precambrian life has a highly incomplete record.
'Swarmed' lacks a precise abundance threshold.
Lowest Silurian in the 1859 text has to be aligned with the modern base of the Cambrian.
Swarmed is qualitative, and the early record is mostly microbial and concentrated in particular facies.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.label: Successive formations are separated by wide intervals of unrecorded time
claims.statement: The chief cause of the imperfection of the geological record is that successive geological formations are separated from each other by wide intervals of time during which no record was left.

operationalizations.text: Calculate the distribution of hiatus durations (unconformities separating successive lithostratigraphic units) and completeness fractions across regional and continental sedimentary columns in quantitative chronostratigraphic databases.

Quantify hiatus durations between mapped sedimentary packages and decompose estimated fossil-record incompleteness among nondeposition or erosion, preservation failure, and sampling. Dominance of long inter-formational hiatuses supports the claim.

Measure hiatus lengths between successive fossiliferous formations and compare them with the durations of the formations themselves. Gaps as long as or longer than the recorded intervals support wide unrecorded separations; continuously recorded succession would count against that pattern. Ranking gaps as the chief cause requires comparing their contribution with other biases.

obstacles: Macrostrat's deepest package-level coverage is strongest in North America, the Caribbean, New Zealand, and deep-sea cores, though global compilations and Sadler completeness datasets confirm the pattern worldwide.
The relative importance of causes varies by region and taxon.
Hiatus duration and fossil incompleteness have correlated estimation errors.
Macrostrat coverage is much denser in some continents than worldwide.
Calling gaps the chief cause requires a model that partitions incompleteness among erosion, non-deposition, facies, and collection bias.
Unconformities can be brief locally and still look wide in a compiled column.

claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: A group's existence is continuous and it never reappears after disappearing
claims.statement: Genera and families, like species, exist continuously from their first to last appearance and do not reappear after they have once disappeared, since their members must form an unbroken succession of generations.

operationalizations.text: Test whether genera and families defined in paleontological databases are monophyletic and stratigraphically continuous once sampling probabilities are accounted for, or whether apparent polyphyletic re-appearances reflect convergent grades that fail phylogenetic monophyly tests.

For genera and families, identify gaps between dated occurrences and estimate sampling-adjusted probabilities of true absence. Confirm continuity when gap lengths match expected non-detection; validated extinction followed by renewed membership would refute it.

Measure internal gaps in genus and family ranges and ask whether any group is genuinely absent from a well-sampled interval and then resumes. Persistent occurrence at low density would support continuity; a well-sampled absence followed by return of the same group would challenge it.

obstacles: Modern cladistic taxonomy explicitly enforces monophyly, making the continuity of natural groups partly definitional unless evaluated on legacy pre-cladistic taxa.
Higher-taxon boundaries are revised over time.
Poor sampling can create false disappearance and reappearance.
If groups are treated as clades, continuity through time is close to a definition and the test loses force.
Lazarus gaps from uneven collecting dominate apparent disappearances and returns.

claims.label: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish
claims.statement: Over geological time small genera have often increased greatly in number of species, and large genera have often reached a maximum, declined and disappeared.

operationalizations.text: Track species richness per genus across stratigraphic stage bins in the fossil record; test whether genus diversity trajectories routinely exhibit wax-and-wane (hat-shaped) curves—expanding from a single founder species to a maximum and subsequently declining to extinction.

Reconstruct genus richness through stratigraphic time from fossil occurrences and estimate transitions from small to large and trajectories after peak richness. Frequent large expansions of initially small genera and peak-to-extinction declines support the claim.

From occurrence counts in time bins, reconstruct genus-richness trajectories and estimate how often small genera later become much richer and how often rich genera peak, decline, and disappear. Those two frequencies being high, after sampling standardization, would support the geological generalization; trajectories dominated by flat or monotonically biased richness would count against it.

obstacles: Rock volume availability and sampling intensity vary across geological stages, requiring subsampling (e.g., Shareholder Quorum Subsampling) to avoid artificial peaks and declines.
Preservation and collection effort vary through time.
Genus concepts change taxonomically.
Uncorrected richness rises toward the present because of rock area and preservation, independent of true diversification.
Last occurrences are smeared backward by incomplete sampling.
Shelly marine animals dominate the usable record, so plants and terrestrial genera are a biased remainder.

claims.label: Zones of overlap between representative species are narrow
claims.statement: Where closely allied or representative species replace each other over a continuous area, the neutral territory between them is generally narrow compared with the territory occupied by each, and species become somewhat abruptly rarer towards their range limits.

operationalizations.text: For parapatric sister species and representative species pairs replacing each other along latitudinal, elevational, or bathymetric gradients, calculate the width of the geographic/elevational zone of sympatry (contact/hybrid zone) as a fraction of the total range span of each species, and measure abundance density profiles approaching the contact zone.

Estimate range widths and overlap-zone widths for geographically replacing close relatives, and fit abundance changes toward each boundary. Overlap zones consistently narrow relative to each range and abrupt edge declines support the claim; broad overlap or gradual transitions refute it.

For sister or representative species, measure the width of the zone where both occur relative to each species' range, and the steepness of abundance decline at the edge. Narrow contact zones and abrupt abundance drops would confirm the claim; overlap widths that are a large fraction of range width, or gradual declines, would refute it.

obstacles: Spatial grid resolution of range maps can artificially inflate apparent overlap unless point-occurrence or transect data (e.g. eBird checklists, elevational transects) are used.
Occurrence density reflects observer effort as well as abundance.
Hybrid zones and patchy habitat complicate a single overlap-width measure.
Abundance, needed for abrupt rarity, is dense for birds and coarse for most other groups.
Depth zonation and deep-sea sister species are sparsely sampled.
Taxonomic splitting can manufacture narrow contacts between newly named species.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.label: Apparent sudden origin of groups reflects missing earlier records
claims.statement: The apparently sudden appearance of whole groups of allied species in a formation is generally an artefact: such groups existed and multiplied earlier, elsewhere or during unrecorded intervals, so older fossils of them should continue to be found.

operationalizations.text: Compare historical first-appearance datums (FADs) of genera, families, and orders across successive editions of global fossil compilations or discovery-year records to test whether continued sampling systematically pushes first appearances into older strata, and compare stratigraphic FADs with phylogenetic ghost lineage durations.

For genera and families, compare first appearances through successive database releases and model range extensions against sampling intensity. The claim is supported if improved sampling systematically pushes inferred origins earlier and reveals pre-radiation occurrences.

Compare present first-appearance dates of genera and families with the dates in earlier compilations, and with the level at which each group becomes diverse. Continued discovery of substantially older fossils supports the claim; first appearances that stay fixed after dense sampling of older rocks count against it.

obstacles: Some rapid diversifications reflect genuine evolutionary radiations rather than purely preservational artefacts.
Taxonomic revisions over time alter the definition of higher groups independently of new fossil discoveries.
Absence below a boundary is intrinsically hard to distinguish from non-preservation.
Database revision history is not a controlled sampling experiment.
A continued absence of older fossils can be attributed to remaining gaps in the record.
Rock availability and collecting effort are uneven below the horizons where a group is already known.

claims.label: Species in large genera differ from one another by small amounts
claims.statement: In large genera the amount of difference between species is often exceedingly small, so that their species resemble varieties more than do species of small genera.

operationalizations.text: Compute mean nearest-neighbor genetic distance (e.g., COI/ITS/rbcL divergence or patristic distance) and morphological distance between congeneric species as a function of genus species richness across plants and insects.

Compare standardized pairwise genetic and morphological distances among species in large versus small genera, with phylogenetic age and sampling controls. Smaller within-genus distances in large genera support the claim.
Regress mean pairwise morphological or genetic distance among congeners on genus richness. Smaller distances in larger genera would support the pattern; equal or larger distances would refute it.

obstacles: Taxonomic splitting bias can artificially produce large genera with tiny interspecific differences if taxonomists working on certain groups split more finely.

claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: New species have appeared slowly and successively on land and in the sea
claims.statement: New species have appeared very slowly and one after another, both on land and in the waters, rather than in simultaneous batches.

operationalizations.text: Test whether first appearances of terrestrial and marine fossil species are distributed across stratigraphic intervals rather than concentrated exclusively at discrete stage boundaries, after controlling for sequence-stratigraphic hiatuses and sampling intensity.

Estimate taxon first-appearance rates and clustering through time separately for terrestrial and aquatic records after standardizing sampling. Compare gradual asynchronous origination against simultaneous pulses at available temporal resolution.

In terrestrial and marine occurrence data, test whether first appearances are spread across successive time bins or clustered in the same short horizons. A staggered sequence supports successive appearance; repeated pulses of many unrelated first appearances, beyond sampling spikes, would challenge it.

obstacles: Unconformities and stage-level binning in global databases artificially cluster first appearances at interval boundaries.

Stage-level dating can make gradual appearances look simultaneous.

Geological stages are coarser than one-after-another within a formation.
The record is mostly genera, so species-level succession is a proxy.
The terrestrial record is much patchier than the marine record, and bedding-scale collecting spikes imitate simultaneous origin.
